extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers, especially novelists looking to add or improve subplots
extracted.subtask_description: Practical techniques and standards for creating, integrating, and managing subplots in a novel so the overall plot feels tightly woven, realistic, and satisfying. Covers purpose, pre-writing, seven distinct subplot structures, clue-planting for mystery, and revision tactics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functions of subplots
rubrics_metrics.description: Think of subplots as simply strands of stories that support or drive the main plot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Subplots can: advance your story in satisfying increments; unleash transformative forces on your main characters (growth or corruption, gain or loss); reveal information to main characters or to the reader; pivot your action and provide twists; speed up or slow down your story’s pace; induce mood (menace, comedy, pathos, triumph); patch holes in (or solve other problems with) your main plot; insert—or challenge!—a moral lesson. They also bring realism by interrupting the flow because life doesn’t move forward all at once.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spinning subplots (do pre-work)
rubrics_metrics.description: Work out your subplots as fully as you can before integrating them into your main plot; treat them as threads you spin before weaving.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Begin by asking: What do I want to accomplish with this subplot? What do I need? What do I want? What would be fun to work with? Brainstorm characters who could populate and propel your plot; write out subplots more or less sequentially so threads are ready before weaving. This helps you avoid ad hoc or aimless subplots.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Isolated Chunk
rubrics_metrics.description: A subplot presented as a distinct episode or side trip—start a new section or chapter and tell a self-contained story-within-a-story, then return to the main narrative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don’t worry about transitions; just write the separate episode. Especially useful in first-person narratives where the narrator can experience only one thing at a time. Classic example: episodic/picaresque sequences in The Adventures of Huckleberry Finn. Use when a subplot can work as a side trip for your main character.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Parallel Line
rubrics_metrics.description: A subplot that runs separately from the main plot and may never touch it, or only converges at the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Start the main plot, then insert the second plot and cut back and forth evenly to emphasize symmetry or contrast. Make the parallel plot any size relative to the main plot; if minor, give it less real estate. Example: Frederick Forsyth’s The Day of the Jackal (Jackal vs. police inspector). Useful for protagonist-antagonist structures and thrillers.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Swallowtail
rubrics_metrics.description: Launch two parallel plots that always converge and interact for a substantial portion of the story, creating suspense as they move toward a joint point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternate between the paths so readers wonder how they’ll connect; when they mesh, both plots gain complexity and reader satisfaction. Joint points can be a place, person, family, or event. Note: alternating more than three parallel plots risks confusing the reader.

rubrics_metrics.name: The In-and-Out
rubrics_metrics.description: Subplots whose characters 'dip in and out' of the protagonist’s life—each incident can be a complete little story that humanizes or informs main characters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Let subplots shuttle as needed: bring a character in for advice, send them off, bring them back later possibly with trouble. In first-person narratives you can drop in chapters written in third person to show action outside the narrator’s range. Example: Scout’s interleaving subplots in To Kill a Mockingbird.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Bookend
rubrics_metrics.description: Introduce a subplot early, leave it dormant for most of the book, then resolve it near the end so readers are rewarded by a late payoff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Essentially a variation of the Isolated Chunk—insert two chunks separated by most of the book. Provide a bit of foreshadowing in the middle so the late resolution feels earned and delightful; this is good to wrap up after the main plot to give readers a place to collect themselves and savor restoration of order.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Bridge Character
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a character who connects two otherwise separate worlds, allowing a subplot to link into the main narrative organically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Invent a character who occupies a separate world or start with the two worlds you want to bridge and create someone who can connect them. Roles like doctors, lawyers, counselors, and clergy often work well because people tell them secrets. Example: a doctor in debt connecting to the streets via an addict who doctor-shops.

rubrics_metrics.name: The Clue (for mysteries, suspense, thrillers)
rubrics_metrics.description: Strategically plant clues to propel puzzle-unraveling and entertain readers; distinguish between clues intended for the fictional sleuth and clues intended for the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plant clues early and often. If you want readers to detect the clue, plan from the ending backward—decide how the crime was done and insert verifiable hints (e.g., an academic detail, a plumbing remodeling) that an astute reader could follow. An author may also place clues only for the sleuth (not the reader). Use imagination but be mindful of fairness to readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managing subplot scope and placement (Finishing the Fabric)
rubrics_metrics.description: Revise subplots so they don’t interrupt the narrative for too long or become unwieldy; break, disperse, or reassign subplot material as needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a subplot interrupts too long, break it into pieces and disperse them; invent additional characters to carry portions; use jump cuts between plot and subplot; let it sit a day then re-read. These tactics help integrate subplots smoothly and tighten the weave of the novel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical limits and anti-patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: Beware of overcomplicating with too many parallel plots or subplots that don’t serve clear purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternating more than three parallel plots risks confusing the reader. Avoid subplots that exist only to be colorful—each subplot should have a purpose (see 'Functions of subplots') and be spun and integrated thoughtfully. If a subplot is unwieldy, revise it as described in 'Finishing the Fabric.'
